title: Ativan and Alcohol: Why Lorazepam and Drinking Do Not Mix
excerpt: Why Ativan (lorazepam) and alcohol shouldn't be mixed: how both slow the brain and breathing, how long lorazepam lasts, why hospitals use it for withdrawal, and when to call 911.
metaDescription: Is it safe to drink on Ativan (lorazepam)? How the two slow breathing, how long lorazepam lasts, hangover anxiety, and the signs that mean call 911.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** don't drink alcohol while you're taking Ativan. Ativan (lorazepam) and alcohol both slow the brain down through the same chemical system, and together they add up to more sedation, more memory loss, and slower breathing than either one alone. Most people who have a drink on the same day as a single small dose won't end up in the hospital, but there is no amount of alcohol that is known to be safe with lorazepam, and the official prescribing information tells patients to avoid it. If you've been prescribed Ativan, the simplest safe rule is no alcohol on the days you take it, and a short conversation with your prescriber about what that means for your situation.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink on a day you take Ativan, and don't take Ativan after you've been drinking, including the next morning if you still feel the alcohol. Never use Ativan to calm hangover anxiety or to help you sleep after a night out. Never take a lorazepam pill that didn't come from a pharmacy. If someone has mixed the two and is very hard to wake, breathing slowly or with long pauses, or has blue or gray lips, **call 911 right away.**

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains how Ativan and alcohol interact and what the official labeling says. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history, and it does not give dosing advice. **Talk to your prescriber** about alcohol before you start Ativan, if you've already been drinking while taking it, or if you want to stop either one. Don't stop lorazepam suddenly on your own if you've been taking it regularly. **Call 911 immediately if** someone who has mixed Ativan and alcohol can't be woken, is breathing slowly, shallowly, or with long pauses, has blue or gray lips or fingertips, is having a seizure, or is vomiting while drowsy or confused. In the US, Poison Control is **1-800-222-1222** for non-emergency questions.

## What Ativan Is and Why People Ask About Alcohol

Ativan is the brand name for **lorazepam**, a prescription medicine in the **benzodiazepine** family. It's the same family as Xanax (alprazolam), Valium (diazepam), and Klonopin (clonazepam). Doctors prescribe lorazepam for anxiety, for short-term help with anxiety-related sleep problems, before medical procedures to calm people down, and in hospitals to stop seizures. It comes as tablets, an injection used in hospitals, and in the US an extended-release capsule sold under a different brand name.

Because lorazepam is so widely prescribed, a lot of people taking it also drink socially. The questions that come up are practical: Can I have a glass of wine at dinner? How long after my dose can I drink? What if I already did? Is it okay the next day? This guide answers each one, and the short version of every answer points the same way, because the chemistry doesn't change from one situation to the next.

## How Ativan and Alcohol Interact: The Brain Chemistry in Plain Words

Your brain has a built-in brake pedal called **GABA**. It's a chemical messenger that calms nerve cells down. When GABA attaches to its main receptor, called the **GABA-A receptor**, it makes the nerve cell less likely to fire. More GABA activity means a quieter, slower brain: first relaxed, then sleepy, then, at high enough levels, unconscious.

- **Ativan presses the brake harder.** Lorazepam attaches to the GABA-A receptor at its own site and makes the receptor respond more strongly every time GABA arrives. That's how it eases anxiety and makes people drowsy.
- **Alcohol presses the same brake.** Alcohol also boosts GABA-A activity, and it dampens the brain's main "go" signal (a chemical called glutamate) at the same time.

When you take both, you're pressing one brake pedal with two feet. The effects don't just sit side by side. They stack, and sometimes they stack more steeply than you'd guess from either one alone. The parts of the brain that keep you breathing automatically, especially while you're asleep, are among the systems that get slowed.

That's the main danger. It isn't liver damage or a chemical reaction in the bottle. It's **too much slowing of the brain and breathing at the same time**, often while someone is asleep and nobody is watching.

### A detail that's specific to lorazepam

Many benzodiazepines, including Xanax and Valium, are broken down by liver enzymes from the cytochrome P450 family. Lorazepam is different. The liver mostly attaches it to another molecule (a process called glucuronidation) and the kidneys clear it, and it doesn't produce active leftover compounds the way diazepam does. This is one reason hospitals often choose lorazepam for older patients or people with some liver problems.

Some websites take that fact and conclude lorazepam is "safer" with alcohol. It isn't. The liver pathway matters for how long the drug lasts and how it interacts with other medicines. It does nothing to change the main problem, which happens in the brain: two substances hitting the same brake at once.

## What the Official Label and Research Say

**The FDA boxed warning.** Ativan carries a boxed warning, the FDA's strongest kind. It covers the serious risks of combining benzodiazepines with opioids (profound sedation, slowed breathing, coma, and death), and since 2020 it also covers abuse, misuse, and addiction, and the risks of physical dependence and withdrawal. Alcohol isn't named in the box itself, but it's covered in the label's warnings about other central nervous system depressants, and patients are told to avoid alcohol while taking lorazepam. The logic is the same as with opioids: two things that slow breathing are more dangerous together.

**Real-world harm data.** Emergency department and overdose studies in the US have repeatedly found that benzodiazepine-related emergencies and deaths usually involve another substance, most often opioids or alcohol, rather than a benzodiazepine on its own. Benzodiazepines alone are rarely fatal in healthy adults. Combined with other depressants, they are a well-known contributor to accidental overdoses.

**Impairment research.** Laboratory studies on volunteers have shown that lorazepam and alcohol together impair memory, reaction time, and coordination more than either one at the same dose alone. Lorazepam is one of the benzodiazepines most associated with memory gaps (doctors call this anterograde amnesia, meaning you don't form new memories for a while). Alcohol does the same thing. Together, blackouts become much more likely.

The consistent message: **lorazepam is a useful medicine on its own, and the danger comes mostly from combining it with other depressants, alcohol included.**

## What Happens If You Mix Ativan and Alcohol?

There's a wide range of possible effects, and the problem is that you can't reliably predict where you'll land on it. It depends on the dose, how much you drank, how close together they were, your body size, whether you ate, your age, and whether anything else sedating is involved, such as sleep aids, antihistamines, gabapentin, or opioids.

| Level | What it can look like |
|---|---|
| Mild | Much stronger drowsiness than expected, feeling "heavy," slower thinking, poor balance |
| Moderate | Slurred speech, stumbling, confusion, large memory gaps, falling asleep mid-conversation, unusual behavior you don't remember later |
| Severe | Very hard to wake, slow or irregular breathing, choking on vomit, very low blood pressure, coma |

Other real-world risks that don't show up in a lab:

- **Falls and injuries.** Lorazepam already raises fall risk, especially in older adults. Add alcohol and the risk goes up.
- **Driving.** Both impair driving on their own. Together they make it far worse, and you may feel more alert than you are.
- **Doing things you don't remember.** Because both cause memory gaps, people sometimes take extra pills or keep drinking without recalling the first ones.

### "I only had one drink"

This is the most common real-world question. A single drink with a low, regular dose of lorazepam is less likely to cause a crisis than a night of heavy drinking. But "less likely" isn't the same as safe, and the official guidance doesn't give an exception for one drink. One glass of wine can make you noticeably drowsier and more unsteady than usual. If it's already happened and you feel okay, don't take more of either, don't drive, and don't sleep alone if you feel unusually sedated. If you're prescribed lorazepam long term and want to know whether occasional light drinking is ever acceptable for you, that's exactly the conversation to have with your prescriber.

## How Long After Taking Ativan Can You Drink?

There's no official waiting period that applies to everyone, and you should be wary of any website that gives you a precise number of hours.

What we do know: lorazepam taken by mouth usually reaches its peak level in the blood about two hours after a dose, and its average half-life (the time it takes the body to clear half of it) is around 12 hours in healthy adults, with real variation from person to person. It typically takes several half-lives for a drug to be mostly gone. So a meaningful amount of lorazepam can still be in your body the next day, even after you stop feeling calm or sleepy.

Things that can make it last longer:

- Older age
- Kidney or significant liver problems
- Taking it regularly rather than once, since levels build up
- Higher doses

If you take Ativan at night to sleep, it's still in your system the next evening to some degree. That's one reason prescribers generally say to avoid alcohol for the whole time you're taking it rather than trying to time doses around drinks. Your pharmacist can give you a far better answer for your specific dose and schedule than any general rule.

## How Long After Drinking Can You Take Ativan?

The same logic runs the other way. Your body clears alcohol at roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot. After a heavy night, alcohol can still be in your blood well into the next morning, even after you've slept.

If you take lorazepam while alcohol is still on board, you're combining them, just in the reverse order. A sensible rule is that if you can still feel the alcohol, or you drank heavily the night before, it's not the time to take Ativan without asking your doctor or pharmacist first. If you take it on a fixed schedule for a medical reason and you've been drinking, call your pharmacist or prescriber for guidance rather than guessing or doubling up later.

## Can You Take Ativan for a Hangover or Hangover Anxiety?

It's a bad idea, for three reasons.

1. **Alcohol may still be in your system.** The morning after heavy drinking, you may not be sober yet. Taking lorazepam then is still combining the two.
2. **Hangover anxiety is partly a rebound from the alcohol itself.** Alcohol boosts GABA while you're drinking. As it wears off, your brain swings the other way for a while, which can leave you jittery, anxious, and on edge. Covering that rebound with another drug that acts on the same system can set up a pattern that's hard to break. Our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) explains this rebound and what tends to help.
3. **It can hide a more serious problem.** In people who drink heavily every day, shakiness, sweating, a racing heart, and strong anxiety the morning after can be early signs of **alcohol withdrawal**, not a hangover. That needs a doctor. We cover the difference in our guide to [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes).

The same goes for using Ativan to get to sleep after a night out. Alcohol already disrupts sleep later in the night, and our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) covers safer ways to handle that.

## "But Doctors Give Ativan for Alcohol Withdrawal"

This confuses a lot of people, so it deserves a clear explanation.

It's true: benzodiazepines, including lorazepam, are a standard hospital treatment for **alcohol withdrawal**. When someone who has been drinking heavily every day suddenly stops, their brain has adapted to constant alcohol pressing on the GABA brake. Without it, the brain becomes overexcited. That can cause tremors, sweating, anxiety, hallucinations, seizures, and a dangerous state called delirium tremens. Benzodiazepines calm that overexcitement because they act on the same system alcohol did.

The key difference is that **this happens after the alcohol is gone, under medical supervision, with dosing guided by repeated checks of symptoms and vital signs.** Doctors are replacing the alcohol's effect in a controlled way and then tapering it, not stacking lorazepam on top of alcohol that's still in the blood. That's the opposite of mixing them on a night out.

If you drink heavily most days and want to cut back or stop, don't try to manage withdrawal yourself with leftover pills. Alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous, and a doctor can plan it safely.

## Ativan vs. Xanax, Valium, and Klonopin With Alcohol

People sometimes ask whether one benzodiazepine is "safer" to drink on than another. The honest answer is no. They all act on the same GABA-A receptor, and they all carry the same core risk with alcohol: added sedation, memory loss, and slowed breathing.

The differences are mostly about timing:

| Medicine | Generic name | General duration |
|---|---|---|
| Xanax | alprazolam | Fast-acting, shorter to intermediate half-life |
| Ativan | lorazepam | Intermediate half-life, around 12 hours on average |
| Klonopin | clonazepam | Longer half-life |
| Valium | diazepam | Long, with active breakdown products that last even longer |

A longer-lasting drug means a longer window during which drinking still means combining. For a deeper look at the most commonly searched one, see our guide to [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol). Similar stacking concerns apply to other sedating medicines, which we cover in [gabapentin and alcohol](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol).

## Warning Signs: When to Call 911

This box is the most important part of the page. If you're reading this because someone has mixed Ativan and alcohol, check for these signs now.

**Call 911 immediately if the person:**

- Can't be woken up, or wakes only briefly and drifts off again
- Is breathing very slowly, shallowly, or with long pauses, or is making gurgling or snoring sounds they don't normally make
- Has blue or gray lips, fingertips, or skin
- Has a very slow pulse or feels cold and clammy
- Is having a seizure
- Is vomiting while drowsy or confused

**While you wait for help:**

- Stay with them. Don't let them "sleep it off" alone.
- If they're breathing but not responsive, roll them onto their side so they won't choke if they vomit.
- If there's any chance opioids or a non-pharmacy pill are involved, give **naloxone** (Narcan) if you have it. It won't reverse lorazepam or alcohol, but it can reverse an opioid, and counterfeit pills sometimes contain fentanyl.
- Tell responders exactly what was taken, how much, and when, if you know.

For non-emergency questions, such as "I took my normal dose and then had a beer, what should I watch for?", call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** in the US. They're free, confidential, and available around the clock.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

The Ativan and alcohol combination carries extra risk if you:

- Are **65 or older**, since lorazepam lasts longer and falls are more dangerous
- Have **sleep apnea**, COPD, or another breathing condition
- Take **opioids**, sleep medicines, sedating antihistamines, muscle relaxants, or gabapentin
- Have **kidney or significant liver disease**
- Take lorazepam **regularly** rather than occasionally
- Drink heavily or binge drink

If any of these apply to you, ask a pharmacist to review your full medication list. Our [medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) is a general starting point, but it doesn't replace that conversation.

## Questions to Ask Your Prescriber

If you drink socially and you've been prescribed Ativan, these are fair, ordinary questions to bring to your next appointment. Doctors would much rather hear them than find out later.

- "How long does my dose stay in my system?"
- "If I'm only taking it as needed, how should I handle a day I plan to drink?"
- "Is there an option for my anxiety or sleep that doesn't interact with alcohol as much?"
- "If I want to stop taking it, how do we taper safely?"

Being honest about how much you drink helps your prescriber choose the right medicine and the right plan. It isn't a confession. It's information they need.

## A Better Path for Social Drinkers

If you're looking up "Ativan and alcohol," you're probably trying to fit a prescription around a normal social life. The most reliable approach is the boring one: skip alcohol on days you take lorazepam, and on days you do drink, drink less, drink slower, eat first, and alternate with water. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence. If anxiety after drinking is the real issue, our article on [alcohol and anxiety](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-anxiety-breaking-the-cycle-naturally-2025) is worth a read.

Some people add supplements around drinking. Here's an honest view of the one this site focuses on:

- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol and the liver. In animal studies, it appears to act partly at GABA-A receptors, the same system lorazepam works on, and how it interacts with benzodiazepines in people hasn't been studied. That means **if you take Ativan, check with your prescriber or pharmacist before trying DHM.** There is no good evidence that DHM or any supplement makes it safe to combine lorazepam and alcohol. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.

No supplement should change how you use a prescription. Follow your prescriber's instructions and the alcohol warning, whatever else you take.

## The Bottom Line

- Ativan (lorazepam) and alcohol both slow the brain through the GABA system, and together they can cause heavy sedation, blackouts, and dangerously slow breathing.
- There's no amount of alcohol known to be safe with lorazepam, and the label tells patients to avoid it.
- Lorazepam's average half-life is around 12 hours, so it can still be in your system the next day.
- Don't use Ativan for hangover anxiety or to sleep after drinking.
- Hospital use for alcohol withdrawal happens after the alcohol is gone and under supervision. It is not a reason to think the two are compatible.
- If someone who mixed them is hard to wake or breathing slowly, call 911.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Ativan?**

No. Ativan (lorazepam) and alcohol both slow the brain through the same GABA system, and together they can cause heavy sedation, memory loss, and dangerously slow breathing. There's no amount of alcohol known to be safe with lorazepam, and the prescribing information tells patients to avoid alcohol. Talk to your prescriber about how to handle drinking before it comes up.

**How long after taking Ativan can I drink?**

There's no official waiting period that applies to everyone. Lorazepam's average half-life is around 12 hours in healthy adults, and it usually takes several half-lives for a drug to be mostly cleared, so a meaningful amount can still be in your body the next day. Older adults, people with kidney or liver problems, and people who take it regularly may clear it more slowly. Ask your pharmacist or prescriber for advice on your specific dose.

**Is lorazepam safer with alcohol than Xanax?**

No. Lorazepam is broken down differently in the liver than alprazolam, but that doesn't change the main risk, which happens in the brain. Both act on the same GABA-A receptor and add to alcohol's effects on sedation, memory, and breathing. Lorazepam also tends to last somewhat longer in the body than immediate-release Xanax.

**Can I take Ativan for hangover anxiety?**

It's a bad idea. Alcohol may still be in your blood the morning after, so you'd still be combining them. Hangover anxiety is partly a rebound from the alcohol itself, and treating it with another depressant can set up a risky pattern. In people who drink heavily every day, morning shakiness and anxiety can also be early alcohol withdrawal, which needs a doctor rather than self-treatment.

**Why do hospitals give Ativan for alcohol withdrawal if it's dangerous with alcohol?**

In withdrawal, the alcohol is already gone and the brain is overexcited because it adapted to constant alcohol. Lorazepam calms that overexcitement under medical supervision, with dosing guided by repeated checks of symptoms and vital signs, and is then tapered. That's very different from taking it on top of alcohol that's still in your system.

**What should I do if I already mixed Ativan and alcohol?**

Don't take more of either one, don't drive, and don't stay alone if you feel unusually drowsy. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US) for advice. Call 911 right away if someone can't be woken, is breathing slowly or with long pauses, has blue or gray lips, is having a seizure, or is vomiting while drowsy or confused.

**Does Ativan have a boxed warning about alcohol?**

Ativan has an FDA boxed warning about combining benzodiazepines with opioids and about abuse, misuse, addiction, dependence, and withdrawal. Alcohol is covered in the label's warnings about other central nervous system depressants, which tell patients to avoid alcohol. The reasoning is the same: two substances that slow breathing are more dangerous together.

**Can I take DHM if I'm on Ativan?**

Check with your prescriber or pharmacist first. In animal studies, DHM appears to act partly at GABA-A receptors, the same system lorazepam works on, and its interaction with benzodiazepines in people hasn't been studied. There's also no good evidence that DHM or any supplement makes it safe to combine Ativan and alcohol.
